questions.q: How many 4-digit numbers can be formed using the digits $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$ without repetition?
questions.answer: The number of permutations of 6 distinct digits taken 4 at a time is $^6P_4 = 6 \times 5 \times 4 \times 3 = 360$.

questions.q: In how many ways can 7 runners finish 1st, 2nd, and 3rd in a race, assuming no ties?
How many even 3-digit numbers can be formed using digits $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ without repetition?
questions.answer: The last digit must be even: 2 choices (2 or 4). Remaining 2 digits can be chosen from the other 4 digits in $4 \times 3 = 12$ ways. Total $= 12 \times 2 = 24$.

questions.q: How many distinct arrangements of all the letters in the word $\text{MATHEMATICS}$ are possible?
questions.answer: 11 letters total: M appears 2, A appears 2, T appears 2. Distinct permutations $= \frac{11!}{2!2!2!} = \frac{39916800}{8} = 4,989,600$.

questions.q: In how many ways can 5 boys and 4 girls stand in a line if all 4 girls must stand together?
questions.answer: Treat the 4 girls as a single block: 6 items to arrange ($5! = 120$ ways). Within the block, the 4 girls can be arranged in $4! = 24$ ways. Total $= 120 \times 24 = 2880$? Wait, 5 boys + 1 block = 6 items, $6! = 720$. $720 \times 24 = 17,280$.

questions.q: In how many ways can 6 people sit around a circular table, where rotations are considered equivalent?
questions.answer: Circular permutations of $n$ items $= (n - 1)!$. For 6 people: $(6 - 1)! = 5! = 120$.

questions.q: A committee of 5 is to be chosen from a group of 8 men and 6 women. How many committees are possible if it must contain exactly 3 men and 2 women?
From a group of 10 students, a team of 4 is selected. If the team must include the student council president, how many distinct teams are possible?
questions.answer: The president is fixed, so we choose the remaining 3 team members from the remaining 9 students: $\binom{9}{3} = \frac{9 \times 8 \times 7}{6} = 84$.

questions.q: A team of 4 is selected from 7 boys and 5 girls. How many teams have at least one girl?
questions.answer: Total teams without restriction $= \binom{12}{4} = 495$. Teams with no girls (all boys) $= \binom{7}{4} = 35$. Teams with at least one girl $= 495 - 35 = 460$.

questions.q: How many 5-digit odd numbers greater than 40,000 can be formed using digits $2, 3, 4, 5, 7$ without repetition?
questions.answer: First digit can be 4, 5, or 7. Case 1: First digit is 4 (1 choice). Last digit must be odd from $\{3, 5, 7\}$ (3 choices). Middle 3 digits: $3! = 6$. Total $= 1 \times 3 \times 6 = 18$. Case 2: First digit is 5 or 7 (2 choices). Last digit has 2 odd choices remaining. Middle 3 digits: $3! = 6$. Total $= 2 \times 2 \times 6 = 24$. Wait, sum $= 18 + 24 = 42$ (or if first is 4, 5, 7). Choices adjusted.

questions.q: A delegation of 4 is chosen from 5 teachers and 6 students. In how many ways can this be done if there must be more teachers than students?
questions.answer: Possibilities: (4 teachers, 0 students) or (3 teachers, 1 student). Case 1: $\binom{5}{4} \times \binom{6}{0} = 5 \times 1 = 5$. Case 2: $\binom{5}{3} \times \binom{6}{1} = 10 \times 6 = 60$. Total $= 5 + 60 = 65$.

questions.q: Four cards are drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that all four cards are of the same suit?
questions.answer: Ways to pick 4 cards of one suit $= \binom{13}{4} = 715$. For 4 suits: $4 \times 715 = 2860$. Total 4-card hands $= \binom{52}{4} = 270,725$. Probability $= 2860/270725 = 44/4165 \approx 0.01056$.
